cross_cutting_insights: The agent search API market in 2026 has undergone major restructuring following Microsoft's retirement of Bing Search APIs (Aug 2025). The market now splits into two camps: agent-native search engines built from scratch for AI workloads (Exa, Tavily, Linkup, Parallel), and traditional SERP scrapers providing Google/Bing data (Serper, SerpAPI). Multiple benchmarks (Rhumb AN Score 20-dim, AIMultiple 100-query evaluation) consistently rank Exa (8.7 AN, 14.39 AIM), Tavily (8.6 AN), and Brave (7.1 AN, 14.89 AIM) among top choices, with latency varying 20x from Brave's 669ms to Parallel's 13.6s. The recommended production architecture advocates multi-provider routing: Exa/Tavily for primary neural/agentic research, Brave for speed/cost/independent index, Firecrawl for deep JS-rendered extraction, and Perplexity for quick synthesized answers. MCP support has become standard across major providers. Cost ranges dramatically from ~$0.30/1K (Serper) to ~$16/1K (Tavily advanced), making query routing and caching critical at scale. Key failure modes identified across evaluations: result instability across providers, rate limit handling clarity (only Exa/Tavily/Serper communicate limits clearly enough for agent backoff), and the synthesis vs retrieval paradigm mismatch — Perplexity returns answers not raw results, making it unsuitable for agents that need to reason over raw web data. The CLI/search-tool landscape is equally diverse: Python-heavy social scraping suites (Agent-Reach, last30days-skill) compete with zero-runtime-dependency Rust/Go binaries (search-cli, AutoCLI, ketch, asearch). asearch occupies a unique niche as a Go single binary with session-based workflow management, pluggable backends, and multi-source parallel search — positioning itself between single-binary ketch (code search focus) and Rust giants search-cli (14 modes) and AutoCLI (333 commands).
